Transcript body:
[00:00:08] Maya Chen: ok hi everyone, thanks for joining, quick intros then we'll jump into the repro that Aurelius shared. I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, with Ravi and Jonas on the eng side.
[00:00:22] Elena Torres: hi all, Elena here. we'll try to be concise, we have a production incident when running int8-quantized r50-small-y type models across our NVLink cluster. sometimes p95 latency spikes and more worryingly token-level precision drift for certain prompts.
[00:00:40] Ravi Patel: thanks Elena. a couple clarifying questions up front; when you say "precision drift" do you mean numeric differences vs FP16 baseline or outright hallucinating tokens?
[00:00:51] Priya Iyer: mostly numeric divergence — outputs are the same idea but token probabilities shift and for a prompt subset the model starts preferring different tokens. not full hallucination but subtle quality shift.
[00:01:05] Samir Khan: and from infra side we also saw intermittent CUDA graph replay failures — sometimes graph replay works, sometimes it faults with an illegal memory access in a kernel that only shows up under multi-gpu NVLink combination.
[00:01:19] Jonas Frey: illegal memory access often points to memory fragmentation across NVLink peer-to-peer allocations — or a kernel that assumes contiguous buffers when they were sharded.
[00:01:33] Elena Torres: yes we reproduced it in staging but it's flaky, hence the meeting to walk through the traces we captured.
[00:01:45] [00:02:00] Ravi Patel: ok can you confirm target stack: are you using TRT-LLM compiled int8 kernels via TRT Server or are you using a vLLM path (pytorch kernels) for the quantized runs?
[00:02:12] Priya Iyer: we tried both. TRT-LLM path and a vLLM-like PyTorch fastpath. TRT-LLM had the highest throughput but showed those occasional precision shifts. vLLM path was slightly slower but more stable in a couple runs.
[00:02:30] Maya Chen: good, that's consistent with what we've seen in field — kernel specialization in TRT can reorder numerical ops and fuse layers which changes rounding behavior; when you add NVLink fragmentation and fine-grained caching it can amplify quant errors in certain sequences.
[00:02:48] [00:03:10] Samir Khan: we recorded nvprof and nsight but the traces are noisy, we dropped the shared link in the calendar invite: https://redwood.link/aur-nvlink-repro-20261105 (note: link has full traces and a small repro docker).
[00:03:28] Ravi Patel: perfect, we'll pull those. high-level plan: bisect on these dimensions — kernel fusion (TRT compile flags), CUDA graph usage (warm start vs dynamic), NVLink topology (peer mapping), and quantization profiling (calibration set).
[00:03:45] [00:04:00] Elena Torres: question — we run on-prem in a VPC with isolated subnets and SR-IOV enabled NICs; is network topology likely to affect NVLink behavior? I thought NVLink is intra-node.
[00:04:12] Jonas Frey: NVLink is intra-node, but scheduler placement across nodes and PCIe peer-to-peer fallback can matter. also RDMA and HBM pressure from cross-node sharded KV cache can cause memory pressure which looks like NVLink faults.
[00:04:30] Priya Iyer: hmm we do have KV cache sharded across GPUs to reduce prefix recompute. could the sharded cache cause the precision bounce?
[00:04:42] Ravi Patel: yes, two mechanisms: 1) when KV cache is sharded and reassembled, quantized keys/values may get different quantization rounding if sharding changes reduction order; 2) kernel path differences when loading KV into fused attention kernels — TRT fused kernels may perform reorderings that aren't bit-identical to PyTorch kernels.
[00:05:02] [00:05:20] Elena Torres: in our repro we observed the precision shift correlates with when CUDA graphs are replayed after scale-up — like a warm-start / cold-run boundary.
[00:05:30] Maya Chen: we've seen CUDA graph warm-starts mask nondeterminism in allocator state; if graph capture occurs when buffers are fragmented, later replays can hit different base addresses leading to different rounding or float-to-int cast order.
[00:05:48] [00:06:10] Samir Khan: so are we suggesting to avoid CUDA graph capture for int8 production? that would kill performance.
[00:06:19] Ravi Patel: not necessarily avoid. Instead, two-pronged approach: 1) make capture deterministic by preallocating large contiguous GPU buffers before capture (reserve memory), and 2) enforce deterministic quant calibration and same reduction orders — e.g., use per-layer symmetric quantization or set deterministic rounding flags where available.
[00:06:40] Priya Iyer: is there a Redwood-config we can set for persistent KV allocation to avoid fragmentation?
[00:06:51] Jonas Frey: yes in Redwood Dedicated we expose a persistent-kv config that pins large buffers and uses a buddy allocator tuned for NVLink peer access. but on your private on-prem cluster you can replicate by preallocating with CUDA malloc and passing pointers into TRT capture sequence. Jonas to share pseudocode.
[00:07:10] [00:07:30] Ravi Patel: also check cuBLAS and cublasLt versions — we've seen different versions change tensor contraction ordering which affects quantized rounding. what driver and CUDA version are you on?
[00:07:41] Samir Khan: CUDA 12.2, driver 545.xx, cublasLt 12.2.1. We can try 12.1 in a repro.
[00:07:52] Maya Chen: note that TRT-LLM binaries are sometimes built against specific cuBLAS versions; mixing builds can produce subtle diffs. we'll record that as part of bisect.
[00:08:08] [00:08:30] Elena Torres: another observation: when NVLink links are asymmetric because of GPU placement, the fragmentation seems to appear more often. is that a known issue?
[00:08:42] Jonas Frey: yes, NVLink topology matters. if two GPUs have only partial link width between them, certain p2p memcpy paths take PCIe fallback and allocator patterns change. the allocator may put a buffer on a different heap to optimize traffic, which then affects capture base pointers.
[00:09:00] [00:09:20] Priya Iyer: our test cluster is 8x A100 80GB on a DGX-like chassis but the mapping is not perfectly symmetric due to some BIOS settings. we'll share the lspci and nvlink topo output.
[00:09:34] Ravi Patel: perfect. for the TRT vs vLLM diff: can you confirm whether TRT was compiled with layer-fusion enabled (--allow-fuse or TF32/FP16 mixing flags)?
[00:09:46] Priya Iyer: yes fusion enabled. we've also tried disabling tensor fusion but throughput dropped 30%.
[00:09:58] [00:10:20] Maya Chen: that's the usual tradeoff — throughput vs numeric fidelity. We can try targeted partial-fusion: keep fusions that don't change quant rounding order and disable others. Ravi: can you explain how we can selectively disable fusions on TRT?
[00:10:34] Ravi Patel: in TRT-LLM you can tweak the builder flags and use a disable-list for plugins; also you can force per-layer calibration and avoid layer-wise asymmetries. We'll produce a recommended flagset for Aurelius.
[00:10:50] [00:11:15] Elena Torres: question about auditing: we need to capture traces but we have strict SOC2 controls. what data can we share safely?
[00:11:26] Jonas Frey: redact customer data — traces should be capture-level only; you can mask input tokens and only provide kernel names, addresses, timings. Redwood can also sign an NDA and we can spin an ephemeral S3 bucket with encryption via KMS.
[00:11:43] Samir Khan: we'll coordinate with Security. Good.
[00:11:55] [00:12:20] Priya Iyer: one more curious bit — when we force workload onto CPU for calibration runs, the quantized calibrator produces different scale factors vs running on GPU. Is that expected?
[00:12:31] Ravi Patel: calibrator implementations differ. Some use histogram methods that are backend-dependent; floating point accumulators might be fused differently. Always run calibration on a target device and with the same batch/order as production.
[00:12:50] [00:13:10] Elena Torres: ok actionable: we'll extract a small prompt set (20 prompts) that reliably shows the drift, and a 3-utterance warmup sequence that triggers the CUDA graph replay boundary.
[00:13:22] Maya Chen: great. We'll then do a controlled bisect: (A) baseline FP16 vLLM, (B) int8 TRT with fusion on, (C) int8 TRT with fusion flags toggled, (D) TRT with preallocated persistent-kv, (E) TRT with capture after explicit prealloc. We'll compare token-wise diffs and kernel traces.
[00:13:47] [00:14:00] Ravi Patel: plan to run per-run: collect nvprof, nsight, cublas logs, capture CUDA Graph capture/replay markers, and also core dumps if illegal mem access occurs. We'll push a repro runner to the shared repo.
[00:14:18] Priya Iyer: we'll coordinate scheduling; when you bisect, please also test on our 2-node setup where p2p falls back to PCIe. That's when we saw worse behavior.
[00:14:34] Jonas Frey: good point. cross-node behavior can surface different allocator code paths.
[00:14:45] [00:15:00] Elena Torres: quick question on KV precision: is it recommended to store KV in FP16 even when model runs int8?
[00:15:10] Ravi Patel: often yes — storing KV in FP16 preserves dynamic range and avoids repeated quant-dequant noise. If you're using int8 for infer weights, keep KV in FP16 or FP32 if memory allows. That reduces downstream drift.
[00:15:24] Maya Chen: Redwood Optimize has a recommended profile for that: "int8-weights + fp16-kv" which we can share.
[00:15:35] [00:15:50] Samir Khan: that might bump memory by 20% but less than moving away from TRT altogether. We'll test tradeoffs.
[00:15:59] [00:16:20] Ravi Patel: also look at activation quantization — some fused kernels quantize intermediate activations differently. We'll add a metric that logs max abs difference per-layer to help find the exact layer causing drift.
[00:16:37] Maya Chen: ok jumping ahead, when you ran vLLM path and saw more stability, did you use dynamic batching or continuous batching?
[00:16:48] Priya Iyer: vLLM used continuous batching, TRT used microbatching with CUDA graphs for latency targets.
[00:17:00] Ravi Patel: microbatch + CUDA graph + fusion is a complex stack where small nondeterminism accumulates. Continuous batching with a well-tested execution path tends to be more stable but sometimes higher p95. We'll compare.
[00:17:14] [00:17:30] Elena Torres: during repro we saw a stacktrace that pointed to a fused attention plugin. Any suggestions for quick mitigation?
[00:17:39] Jonas Frey: quick mitigation: fall back that attention op to a reference implementation (disable plugin) for the suspect layer during rollout. You can do a gradual canary: 10% traffic on non-fused path. Redwood Console can route a percentage to the fallback.
[00:17:56] Maya Chen: that's a good canary pattern — we can set up an A/B route and capture per-route token-diff metrics.
[00:18:08] [00:18:40] Priya Iyer: one last infra nit: are there configuration knobs to force the allocator to use large page allocations to reduce fragmentation?
[00:18:50] Ravi Patel: yes, use cudaHostAlloc with mapped flags for CPU pinned memory or configure the driver's large page pool. Also, on DGX-like systems you can enable GPU hugepages / MHS tuning via driver knobs. We'll include commands in the runbook.
[00:19:05] Elena Torres: amazing. Anything else before we move to timeline?
[00:19:12] Maya Chen: just to confirm access: Aurelius will upload the masked repro + NVLink topo + traces to the shared link and we will run bisect on a Redwood test cluster and on Aurelius staging cluster.
[00:19:28] [00:19:45] --- mid-call pause for quick screen share of nvprof flamegraphs (not transcribed verbatim) ---

[00:23:50] Priya Iyer: ok that matches what we saw.
[00:24:05] Maya Chen: we'll attach a patch to force alignment to 256 bytes before capture; it's a low-risk change to try.
[00:24:20] [00:24:45] Elena Torres: thanks. On the SOC2 note, we'll get security to sign off on an ephemeral upload mechanism.

[00:25:12] Samir Khan: yes that works for infra.
[00:25:20] Priya Iyer: yes.
